lead: Commutation is the act of turning off a conducting SCR. The anode current must fall below the holding current, and the device must stay reverse-biased long enough to regain forward blocking. In AC circuits the supply voltage does this at every zero crossing; that is natural commutation. In DC circuits an external circuit must force the current down; that is forced commutation. These ideas decide how rectifiers, choppers and inverters release a conducting thyristor, so every converter designer needs them.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for holding current and latching, and Chapter 1.3 for turn-on and gate pulses.

blocks.text: An SCR latches on when gate current starts regeneration. Once anode current exceeds the latching current, the gate loses control. The SCR stays on while anode current is above the holding current I<sub>H</sub>. It turns off only when anode current falls below I<sub>H</sub> and the anode-cathode voltage stays negative for a minimum time. That time lets stored charge in the four layers clear. The process is commutation.

items: Natural commutation happens when the source is AC. At the end of each half cycle the supply current passes through zero, the SCR reverse-biases, and it blocks again. Some syllabi call this line commutation. Class F is the line-commutated case.

Forced commutation happens when the source is DC. The supply current does not fall by itself, so a capacitor, an inductor or a separate pulse must push the SCR current to zero and apply reverse voltage. Classes A to E are forced methods.

sections.h3: Circuit turn-off time and device turn-off time

blocks.text: The circuit gives a reverse-bias window t<sub>c</sub>. The device needs a minimum t<sub>q</sub> from its datasheet. Successful commutation requires t<sub>c</sub> > t<sub>q</sub>. If t<sub>c</sub> is shorter, the SCR has not recovered and may turn on again when forward voltage returns. Bringing current to zero is only the start; the SCR must stay reverse-biased for longer than t<sub>q</sub>.

blocks.where: t<sub>c</sub> is the circuit turn-off time in seconds; C is the commutating capacitance in farads; V is the capacitor voltage at the start of commutation in volts; I is the load current in amperes.

blocks.text: On a waveform, anode current falls to zero and anode voltage goes negative for t<sub>c</sub>. The negative part must extend past t<sub>q</sub>. t<sub>c</sub> is set by the circuit; t<sub>q</sub> is set by the device and its junction temperature. A larger capacitor or a higher capacitor voltage lengthens t<sub>c</sub>, but it also stresses the SCR.

Forced commutation circuits are named by how they create the reverse-bias window. Class A self-commutation uses a series resonant load. The load current is a damped sine and crosses zero on its own. Class B resonant pulse uses an LC circuit that sends a reverse pulse through the SCR. Class C complementary uses two SCRs and a capacitor; turning on one SCR reverse-biases the other. Class D auxiliary uses a second SCR to connect a charged capacitor across the main SCR. Class E external pulse uses a separate voltage or current pulse. Class F line is natural commutation from an AC supply.

figure.caption: Commutation is either natural, where the AC line itself turns the device off (class F), or forced, where extra components or a pulse do it (classes A to E, DC circuits).

spec.aria: Commutation splits into natural commutation, which is class F line commutation on an AC supply, and forced commutation, which covers classes A to E on DC circuits.

examples.question: A capacitor commutation circuit has C = 1 μF charged to 200 V. The load current is 5 A. The SCR datasheet gives t<sub>q</sub> = 30 μs. Find the circuit turn-off time t<sub>c</sub> = C × V / I. Is commutation successful?
steps: Write the given values: V = 200 V and I = 5 A.
Substitute in t<sub>c</sub> = C × V / I = (1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> F × 200 V) / 5 A.
Divide by 5 A: t<sub>c</sub> = 2 × 10<sup>−4</sup> / 5 = 4 × 10<sup>−5</sup> s = 40 μs.
Compare with t<sub>q</sub>: 40 μs > 30 μs, so the reverse-bias window is long enough.
examples.answer: t<sub>c</sub> = 40 μs; since 40 μs > 30 μs, commutation is successful.

C = 1e-6
V = 200.0
I = 5.0
t_c = C * V / I
t_c_us = t_c * 1e6
print(t_c_us)

traps: Natural commutation cannot turn off a DC-fed SCR; the DC current never crosses zero by itself.
Bringing current to zero is not enough. The SCR must stay reverse-biased for longer than t<sub>q</sub>.
Do not confuse t<sub>c</sub> (circuit turn-off time) with t<sub>q</sub> (device turn-off time). t<sub>c</sub> comes from C, V and I; t<sub>q</sub> comes from the datasheet.
Class B is resonant pulse, not load commutation; class A is load or self-commutation.
In a capacitor commutation circuit, use the capacitor voltage after charging, not the supply voltage, in t<sub>c</sub> = C × V / I.

quiz.a: Commutation is turning off a conducting SCR by reducing anode current below holding current and keeping it reverse-biased long enough to regain forward blocking.

quiz.q: Why can natural commutation work only with an AC supply?
quiz.a: An AC supply current falls to zero at each zero crossing and then reverses, so it reverse-biases the SCR without extra circuitry. A DC supply does not create that zero crossing.

quiz.q: A capacitor of 2 μF charged to 150 V commutates a 3 A load. Find t<sub>c</sub>. The SCR needs t<sub>q</sub> = 60 μs. Does it turn off?
quiz.a: t<sub>c</sub> = C × V / I = 2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 150 / 3 = 100 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s = 100 μs. Since 100 μs > 60 μs, yes, it turns off.

quiz.q: A student says, “The SCR turns off as soon as anode current reaches zero.” Correct the statement.
quiz.a: Current zero is only the start. The SCR must remain reverse-biased for t<sub>c</sub> > t<sub>q</sub> so stored charge can clear; otherwise it turns back on when forward voltage returns.

quiz.q: Match class A, B, C, D and E to self, resonant pulse, complementary, auxiliary and external.
quiz.a: Class A is self or load commutation; class B is resonant pulse; class C is complementary; class D is auxiliary; class E is external pulse.

quiz.q: In class C complementary commutation, one SCR is on and the capacitor is charged to 200 V. The load current is 4 A and C = 0.5 μF. Find t<sub>c</sub>.
Why is class F called line commutation?
quiz.a: Because the AC line or supply voltage itself reduces the current to zero and reverse-biases the SCR.

quiz.q: State the condition for successful commutation.
quiz.a: The circuit turn-off time must be longer than the device turn-off time: t<sub>c</sub> > t<sub>q</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, forced commutation circuits are mostly replaced by gate-turn-off devices such as GTO, IGBT and MOSFET, which can be switched off from the gate. Still, the same t<sub>c</sub> > t<sub>q</sub> idea appears in resonant and soft-switching converters, where the circuit creates a zero-voltage or zero-current window. Wide band-gap devices have short t<sub>q</sub>, so layout and gate drive become the limit. Search next for “SCR commutation circuits”, “resonant DC link” and “soft switching turn-off”.
